transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2027-08-29   Time: 15:00 UTC   Duration: ~52m
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Ethan Rivera (Redwood SE), Rajiv Menon (CTO - Cobalt), Sofia Alvarez (ML Eng), Amir Patel (Infra Lead), Lina Gomez (Product)

Optional sections:
Summary: see summary field above.
References: lab report (https://redwood.ai/labs/cobalt-lab-report), spreadsheet (drive link: https://drive.redwood/cobalt/poc-results.xlsx), security deck (internal link shared after call)

Transcript body:
[00:00] Maya: hey everyone, thanks for joining, I think we have about 50 minutes, quick roll call?
[00:12] Rajiv: yeah hi Rajiv here, Sofia, Amir, Lina also on my side.
[00:18] Maya: awesome, Ethan will kick into the bench readout, i'll chime in on commercial and next steps.
[00:24] Ethan: cool, thanks maya. so quick context - we re-ran the head-to-head across your 512 token customer prompts, same input distribution as last week, two main setups: Redwood quantify-path on g5a A10-ish instances and IonixCloud baseline on their default config.
[00:40] Sofia: quick clarification, when you say quantify-path you mean the 4-bit quantize we shipped?
[00:44] Ethan: yeah, it's our 4-bit quant profile with per-channel simd optimizations - sometimes the transcript picks up 'four bit quant', could show as 'for bit'.
[00:55] Amir: and hardware? you said A10, is that the A10G? we run a mix of a10g and v100 in prod right now.
[01:02] Ethan: A10G variant, we matched IonixCloud on their chosen instance class as closely as possible. little variance in clock, but that's in the lab notes.
[01:12] Maya: ok let's go into results.

[01:18] Ethan: top line: p50 latency improved ~18-24% depending on prompt length for the quantized setup w/ adaptive batching enabled. around p95 we saw narrower wins, from 6% up to 12% improvement on most tiers, but there are outliers where their network egress and request tails beat us for certain small batch sizes. our unit cost dropped ~27% after quant and batching.
[01:41] Lina: when you say unit cost is that per token or per inference? we bill per token.
[01:45] Ethan: per token equivalent; spreadsheet has tokenized counts and cost math, but it's approximate — tokens vary with your prompts.
[01:52] Rajiv: i'm worried about p95, our SLA is p95 < 450ms for user-facing chat. what were the exact p95 numbers?
[01:59] Ethan: for 512 tokens, Ionix avg p95 around 410-430ms depending on region; Redwood quant path was 360-390ms in the primary lab region. some tails hit 480ms under bursty concurrency due to network egress and our routing fallback to a lower-memory variant.
[02:16] Sofia: so in those tails is it routing or kv cache warmup?
[02:20] Ethan: a combo. KV cache warmup causes a small bump for repeated long-context sessions; routing fallback effects appear when the autoscaler triggers a cold-start on a node and we temporarily route to a lower-latency but lower-throughput slab.
[02:32] Amir: does that mean a cold start adds 100s of ms? that's a non-starter for us.
[02:36] Ethan: not hundreds, more like 60-120ms for a cold node depending on sequence length — again in our lab logs it's visible. we have suggestions: keep warm pools for your critical routes and set a small reserved dedicated slot.
[02:47] Maya: this is where dedicated capacity helps — reserved slots reduce cold starts and you get predictable throughput.
[02:52] Rajiv: cost tradeoff? reserved slots cost more up front.
[02:55] Maya: yes, there's a commit, but our Optimize module suggests reserved for the 10% of traffic that requires strict p95. the rest can live on hosted with adaptive batching. i'll attach a cost projection.

[03:06] [03:06] Ethan: diving deeper, we also tried prefix caching for the common system prompts — that shaved another 8% off p50 and trimmed some p95 outliers because we avoided re-encoding the same prefix.
[03:18] Sofia: how did Ionix handle prefix caching?
[03:21] Ethan: unclear from their public docs; in our baseline runs we saw less effective prefix reuse which suggested their routing didn't preserve per-session state as aggressively. there may be a transcription of 'Ionix couldn't keep state' in some notes.

[03:33] Lina: security/compliance check — procurement needs SOC2 + KMS integration details. where do we stand?
[03:39] Maya: we have SOC 2 Type II and an enterprise KMS/HSM integration for private deployments. for hosted we offer encryption at rest and in transit, and we can provide pen test reports. i'll share the security deck after the call — note: for a V P C/private deploy we can wrap KMS in your tenant.
[03:52] Amir: for the private path, network peering is a must. we'll need exact egress IPs and rules.
[03:57] Ethan: we'll provide the list; i listed it in the lab appendix but will also provide a hardened one for your infra team.

[04:06] Rajiv: one area we noticed last week was midday latency spikes tied to your autoscaler behavior during bursty loads. any mitigation short-term?
[04:15] Ethan: two quick knobs — reduce scale-in aggressiveness and increase minimum warm replicas for the route; enable burst slots and short-term reservations. those changes were toggled in the lab for the run that produced the narrower p95 gap.
[04:28] Sofia: can you show the run config?
[04:30] Ethan: yes I have the run config in the spreadsheet, lane 3-6, but note the spreadsheet cell labels are a little messy — sometimes the exporter swapped names.

[04:40] [04:40] Maya: commercial note: procurement will want a canary that uses your production peering and our dedicated slot for two weeks. what's realistic?
[04:48] Ethan: we can provision a one-hour canary first using reserved dedicated slot to validate p95 and traces, then extend. provisioning takes roughly 24-48 hours to get the dedicated node reserved in your target region.
[04:58] Amir: we prefer the week of Sep 5, gives us time for firewall rules.
[05:03] Maya: we'll target that.

[05:08] [05:08] Rajiv: about unit cost — you said 27% lower. does that include network egress differences?
[05:13] Ethan: yes, our calc accounts for token compute cost and typical egress, but not bespoke customer network discounts. the spreadsheet has a sensitivity tab with +/- 10% egress variance.
[05:25] Sofia: any caveats on quality after quant? we saw a small hallucination uptick in one prompt cluster last run.
[05:32] Ethan: good flag — we ran evals on your prompt set; on average quality delta was negligible, but one cluster (long legal clauses) had a slight drop; we can pin a higher-precision variant for those prompts via routing rules.
[05:46] Lina: that's promising. product wants to make sure routing is seamless, not manual.
[05:50] Ethan: yes, routing rules can be automated by request signature; we'll show a demo in the canary.

[06:00] [06:00] Sofia: about the traces we'll share — what format do you want?
[06:04] Ethan: OpenTelemetry traces plus raw request/response logs, compressed. please obfuscate any PHI before sharing.
[06:11] Amir: we will, yes.

[06:20] [06:20] Maya: quick commercial timeline — procurement asks security docs, then a two-week canary, then contract. are we aligned?
[06:28] Rajiv: yes but we need the security deck first.
[06:30] Maya: will send by Sep 1.

[06:36] [06:36] Ethan: small note on fallback: we built an automatic fallback to a slightly larger model to keep latency bounded; that increases cost but keeps SLOs. in the lab we only triggered fallback <2% of the time.
[06:51] Sofia: curious, if fallback triggers during heavy load does it cascade?
[06:54] Ethan: we have circuit breakers to avoid cascade; fallback is per-route and we monitor queue lengths.

[07:03] [07:03] Rajiv: can we see a trace sample?
[07:06] Ethan: yes, will attach a trace snippet to the spreadsheet.

[07:12] [07:12] Maya: ok let's go rapid-fire through the appendix numbers in lane 2-4. Ethan, can you summarize the region deltas?
[07:18] Ethan: US-west shows the highest p50 win (24%), US-east slightly lower (18%) due to Ionix's closer edge points in that region. eu-west had similar improvements; apac we didn't run full parity. table in sheet.
[07:33] Lina: do you recommend dedicated in all regions?
[07:36] Ethan: only for regions with strict p95 needs — we recommend reserved slots in US-west and US-east initially.

[07:44] [07:44] Sofia: there was a weird transcription note last time that said 'K V cache leak' — was that real?
[07:51] Ethan: not a leak, more of an eviction pattern where KV cache size dropped under memory pressure; we addressed it by bumping the cache allocation for those workloads.

[08:00] [08:00] Amir: for the canary we need IPs and a temporary BGP announcement?
[08:05] Ethan: we don't do BGP from our side but can provide fixed egress IPs and a peering doc.

[08:12] [08:12] Rajiv: anything else on the p95 tail mitigation?
[08:16] Ethan: keep warm replicas, reserved slots, prefix caching, and reduced scale-in aggressiveness. plus small batching windows to desmooth spikes.

[08:28] [08:28] Maya: ok final wrap — action items and next steps as captured. we'll schedule the canary for the week of Sep 5; security deck and lab spreadsheet to be shared by Sep 1; customer to run 10k load and upload traces; SE to provision quantized job and attach traces.
[08:47] Rajiv: sounds good, thanks everyone.
[08:50] Lina: quick note — procurement might push for a two-week pilot not one hour, just so you know.
[08:55] Maya: understood, we'll be flexible.
[09:00] Amir: thanks all.
[09:02] Maya: thanks, call over.

End of transcript.

Notes on transcription quality: medium — some proper nouns and acronyms mis-recognized (IonixCloud sometimes 'Ionic cloud', K V cache split, V P C typed as letters). Occasional filler words and run-ons preserved.
